claim: Fluoride ion is ubiquitous in soil, water, and marine environments at 10-100 μM levels.
source: Fluoride pervades our biosphere, appearing in groundwater, sea, and soil typically at 10–100 μM levels (Weinstein and Davison, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Weinstein and Davison, 2004

claim: Fluoride ion is a chronic threat to microorganisms.
source: Fluoride ion, ubiquitous in soil, water, and marine environments, is a chronic threat to microorganisms.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge about fluoride toxicity

claim: Fluoride inhibits enolase, an enzyme essential for glycolytic metabolism.
source: This ubiquitous inorganic xenobiotic inhibits two enzymes essential for glycolytic metabolism and nucleic acid synthesis: enolase and pyrophosphatase (Marquis et al., 2003; Samygina et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Marquis et al., 2003 and Samygina et al., 2007

claim: Fluoride inhibits pyrophosphatase, an enzyme essential for nucleic acid synthesis.
source: This ubiquitous inorganic xenobiotic inhibits two enzymes essential for glycolytic metabolism and nucleic acid synthesis: enolase and pyrophosphatase (Marquis et al., 2003; Samygina et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Marquis et al., 2003 and Samygina et al., 2007

claim: Many prokaryotes, archea, unicellular eukaryotes, and plants use Fluc proteins to lower cytoplasmic F− levels.
source: Many prokaryotes, archea, unicellular eukaryotes, and plants use a recently discovered family of F− exporter proteins to lower cytoplasmic F− levels to counteract the anion's toxicity.
evidence: Supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript and citations

claim: Fluc proteins form constitutively open anion channels when purified and reconstituted in liposomes and planar phospholipid bilayers.
source: We show here that these 'Fluc' proteins, purified and reconstituted in liposomes and planar phospholipid bilayers, form constitutively open anion channels with extreme selectivity for F− over Cl−.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from liposome flux assays and planar bilayer recordings shown in Figures 2 and 3

claim: Fluc channels exhibit extreme selectivity for F− over Cl−.
source: We show here that these 'Fluc' proteins, purified and reconstituted in liposomes and planar phospholipid bilayers, form constitutively open anion channels with extreme selectivity for F− over Cl−.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from liposome flux assays and planar bilayer recordings

claim: The active Fluc channel is a dimer of identical or homologous subunits arranged in antiparallel transmembrane orientation.
source: The active channel is a dimer of identical or homologous subunits arranged in antiparallel transmembrane orientation.
evidence: Supported by SEC-SLS data, TIRF photobleaching experiments, Poisson-dump analysis, and fused-dimer experiments shown in Figures 4 and 6

claim: Dual-topology assembly has not previously been seen in ion channels.
source: This dual-topology assembly has not previously been seen in ion channels but is known in multidrug transporters of the SMR family, and is suggestive of an evolutionary antecedent of the inverted repeats found within the subunits of many membrane transport proteins.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of ion channel structures

claim: Dual-topology assembly is known in multidrug transporters of the SMR family.
source: This dual-topology assembly has not previously been seen in ion channels but is known in multidrug transporters of the SMR family, and is suggestive of an evolutionary antecedent of the inverted repeats found within the subunits of many membrane transport proteins.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of SMR transporter structures

claim: CLCF-type proteins are F−/H+ antiporters.
source: Two separate, phylogenetically unrelated families of F− exporters are now known: CLCF-type F−/H+ antiporters, a subclass of the widespread CLC superfamily of anion-transport proteins, and a group of small membrane proteins known as the 'crcB' family or, as we rename them here (to avoid confusion with the CLCs), the 'Fluc' family.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of CLC protein function

claim: Fluc proteins are widespread among unicellular organisms.
source: Fluc proteins are widespread among unicellular organisms.
evidence: Based on genomic analysis and established knowledge

claim: Deletion of the single Fluc gene in Escherichia coli produces hypersensitivity to F−.
source: Deletion of the single Fluc gene in Escherichia coli produces hypersensitivity to F−, and this growth-phenotype may be rescued by F− exporter genes from a variety of bacterial species (Baker et al., 2012; Stockbridge et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baker et al., 2012 and Stockbridge et al., 2012

claim: The F− hypersensitivity phenotype in E. coli Fluc deletion mutants may be rescued by F− exporter genes from a variety of bacterial species.
source: Deletion of the single Fluc gene in Escherichia coli produces hypersensitivity to F−, and this growth-phenotype may be rescued by F− exporter genes from a variety of bacterial species (Baker et al., 2012; Stockbridge et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baker et al., 2012 and Stockbridge et al., 2012

claim: Prokaryotic Fluc sequences consist of 120-130 residues with four predicted transmembrane helix motifs.
source: Prokaryotic Fluc sequences consist of 120–130 residues with four predicted transmembrane (TM) helix motifs (Figure 1A), short N- and C-termini, and a strongly conserved sequence (GxxGGxTTFSTFxxE) in TM3.
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 1A

claim: Fluc proteins have short N- and C-termini.
source: Prokaryotic Fluc sequences consist of 120–130 residues with four predicted transmembrane (TM) helix motifs (Figure 1A), short N- and C-termini, and a strongly conserved sequence (GxxGGxTTFSTFxxE) in TM3.
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 1A

claim: Fluc proteins have a strongly conserved sequence (GxxGGxTTFSTFxxE) in TM3.
source: Prokaryotic Fluc sequences consist of 120–130 residues with four predicted transmembrane (TM) helix motifs (Figure 1A), short N- and C-termini, and a strongly conserved sequence (GxxGGxTTFSTFxxE) in TM3.

claim: Purified Fluc proteins run cleanly on SDS-PAGE near the predicted molecular weights.
source: The purified proteins run cleanly on SDS-PAGE (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) near the predicted molecular weights and migrate on size-exclusion columns (SEC) as monodisperse peaks about 0.6 ml ahead of the expected monomer position (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by SDS-PAGE data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Purified Fluc proteins migrate on size-exclusion columns as monodisperse peaks about 0.6 ml ahead of the expected monomer position.

claim: Ec2 and Bpe are particularly stable, with chromatographic profiles unaltered even after several days in detergent solution at 37°C.
source: Both Ec2 and Bpe are particularly stable, with chromatographic profiles unaltered even after several days in detergent solution at 37°C.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations of protein stability

claim: Fluc proteins are randomly oriented in reconstituted liposomes.
source: Figure 1C shows that Fluc proteins are randomly oriented in the liposomes.
evidence: Supported by protease protection and labeling experiments shown in Figure 1C

claim: About half of the Fluc protein population in liposomes has an externally exposed C-terminus and is susceptible to protease cleavage.
source: About half of the protein population has an externally exposed C-terminus and is susceptible to cleavage, as indicated by faster migration on SDS-PAGE.
evidence: Supported by protease protection experiments shown in Figure 1C

claim: The N- and C-termini of Fluc are exposed on the same side of the membrane.
source: This treatment labels only the lower band containing the polypeptides with externally exposed C-termini, thereby demonstrating that the N- and C-termini are exposed on the same side of the membrane, as anticipated by the Fluc hydropathy profile.

claim: Fluc-mediated F− efflux is so fast that an initial rate measurement is precluded by the 1-s dead-time of the stirred-cuvette system.

claim: The single-Fluc transport rate has a lower limit of ∼30,000 s−1.

claim: The Fluc transport rate is substantially higher than turnover of any conformational-cycle based membrane transporter.
source: Since this is substantially higher than turnover of any conformational-cycle based membrane transporter (Jayaram et al., 2008), it intimates that Fluc might be a F− channel.

claim: Proteoliposomes containing Fluc are selectively permeable to F−.
source: First, the proteoliposomes are selectively permeable to F−; Cl− efflux is undetectable on this timescale, and similar experiments in the absence of F− recapitulate this lack of Cl− transport.
evidence: Supported by liposome flux assay data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Cl− efflux from Fluc-containing proteoliposomes is undetectable on the experimental timescale.
source: First, the proteoliposomes are selectively permeable to F−; Cl− efflux is undetectable on this timescale, and similar experiments in the absence of F− recapitulate this lack of Cl− transport.
evidence: Supported by liposome flux assay data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Fluc-Ec2 insertion into planar bilayers occurs in discrete steps.
source: When fused into planar bilayers, these liposomes evoke a robust increase in bilayer conductance in discrete steps (Figure 2B), each of which reports a single liposome inserting its packet of ion-conducting proteins.
evidence: Supported by planar bilayer recording data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Each discrete conductance step reports a single liposome inserting its packet of ion-conducting proteins.
source: When fused into planar bilayers, these liposomes evoke a robust increase in bilayer conductance in discrete steps (Figure 2B), each of which reports a single liposome inserting its packet of ion-conducting proteins.
evidence: Based on interpretation of planar bilayer recording data

claim: The heterogeneity in step-size reflects the wide distribution of liposome size.
source: The heterogeneity in step-size reflects the wide distribution of liposome size (Miller and Racker, 1976; Accardi et al., 2004).
evidence: Based on established knowledge cited from Miller and Racker, 1976 and Accardi et al., 2004

claim: Fluc-mediated current appears as a 'leak' without any time- or voltage-dependent gating over a wide voltage range.
source: As shown in the inset to Figure 2C, recorded in the presence of a salt gradient (300 mM NaF//30 mM NaF), the current appears as a 'leak' without any time- or voltage-dependent gating over a wide voltage range.
evidence: Supported by planar bilayer recording data shown in Figure 2C inset

claim: The Fluc-mediated conductance is ideally selective for F− over Na+.
source: The Fluc-mediated conductance is ideally selective for F− over Na+, as seen from the zero-current voltage (reversal potential) of 53 mV, indistinguishable from the Nernst potential for F− in the eightfold ionic activity gradient.
evidence: Supported by reversal potential measurements from planar bilayer recordings

claim: The reversal potential under salt-gradient conditions (300 mM NaF//30 mM NaF) is 53 mV.
source: Reversal potentials from 4–5 separate bilayers were 53 ± 1 mV and 119 ± 3 mV for salt-gradient and bi-ionic conditions, respectively.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2C

claim: The reversal potential under bi-ionic conditions (300 mM NaF//300 mM NaCl) is 119 mV.
source: Reversal potentials from 4–5 separate bilayers were 53 ± 1 mV and 119 ± 3 mV for salt-gradient and bi-ionic conditions, respectively.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2C

claim: The F−/Cl− permeability ratio has a lower limit of ∼100.
source: High selectivity is further illustrated by the I–V relation under bi-ionic conditions (300 mM NaF//300 mM NaCl), whose high reversal potential (119 mV) sets a lower limit of ∼100 on the F−/Cl− permeability ratio.
evidence: Based on calculation from reversal potential measurements

claim: Most Fluc insertion-steps are 1.8 pA under the experimental conditions, equivalent to 7 pS.
source: Figure 3A shows examples of Fluc-insertion events in three separate bilayers, along with a histogram of Fluc insertion-step amplitudes taken from ∼50 bilayers (Figure 3B, upper panel). Most of these insertion-steps are 1.8 pA under these conditions, equivalent to 7 pS, while a minority (<20%) are 30–50% of this main step-size (illustrated in the third trace).
evidence: Supported by single-channel recording data shown in Figure 3

claim: A minority (<20%) of Fluc insertion-steps are 30-50% of the main step-size.

claim: The Fluc 'full-open' state persists >95% of the time at all voltages (−200 mV to +200 mV).
source: The 'full-open' state persists >95% of the time at all voltages (−200 mV to +200 mV).
evidence: Supported by single-channel recording analysis

claim: Single Fluc channels display voltage-independent, anion-selective characteristics.
source: These channels display voltage-independent, anion-selective characteristics in harmony with the macroscopic currents reported above, and their appearance is strictly dependent on reconstituting Fluc protein into the liposomes.
evidence: Supported by single-channel recording data

claim: Single-channel appearance is strictly dependent on reconstituting Fluc protein into the liposomes.
source: These channels display voltage-independent, anion-selective characteristics in harmony with the macroscopic currents reported above, and their appearance is strictly dependent on reconstituting Fluc protein into the liposomes.

claim: Single-molecule turnover of Fluc is ∼107 F− ions/sec at −200 mV.
source: Accordingly, we conclude that these unitary current-steps reflect activity of single Fluc proteins, with single-molecule turnover of ∼107 F− ions/sec at −200 mV, a rate typical for ion channels and three to four orders of magnitude higher than the fastest known transporters.
evidence: Based on calculation from single-channel current measurements

claim: Fluc turnover rate is three to four orders of magnitude higher than the fastest known transporters.

claim: Fluc-Ec2 runs as a homodimer in detergent micelles on a size-exclusion column.
source: Fluc-Ec2 runs as a homodimer in detergent micelles on a size-exclusion column, as determined by combined measurements of UV absorbance, refractive index, and static light scattering of the eluting peak (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by SEC-SLS/UV/RI data shown in Figure 4A

claim: The preponderance of single- and double-bleach events in TIRF photobleaching is fully consistent with a dimer architecture.
source: Upon illumination of these liposomes immobilized on a glass surface, the covalently attached fluorophores bleach in several minutes (Figure 4B,C), mostly in single and double steps (Figure 4D). Given the measured labeling efficiency (72%), the preponderance of single- and double-bleach events is fully consistent with a dimer (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by TIRF photobleaching data shown in Figure 4B-E

claim: Fewer than 5% of fluorophores bleach in three or four steps.
source: Fewer than 5% bleach in three or four steps, consistent with co-localization of the liposomes, but not with trimeric or tetrameric architecture for the channel.
evidence: Supported by TIRF photobleaching data shown in Figure 4D

claim: The best exponential fit to the Fluc-Ec2 Poisson-dump data corresponds to a molecular weight of 31.7 kDa for the functional channel.
source: The best exponential fit to the Fluc-Ec2 data corresponds to a molecular weight of 31.7 kDa for the functional channel, in unreasonably good agreement with the predicted size of the homodimer, 31.6 kDa.
evidence: Supported by Poisson-dump analysis shown in Figure 4G

claim: The predicted size of the Fluc-Ec2 homodimer is 31.6 kDa.
source: The best exponential fit to the Fluc-Ec2 data corresponds to a molecular weight of 31.7 kDa for the functional channel, in unreasonably good agreement with the predicted size of the homodimer, 31.6 kDa.

claim: Neither La1 nor La2 alone catalyzes F− efflux from liposomes.

claim: Co-reconstituting both La1 and La2 produces rapid F− efflux.

claim: Twin Flucs possess abundantly charged loops.
source: The twin Flucs possess abundantly charged loops; for one of the pair, a positive charge bias resides on the N- and C-termini and loop 2, while its homologous partner exhibits a converse bias, with excess positive charge on loops 1 and 3 (Figure 5D).

claim: For one of the twin Flucs, a positive charge bias resides on the N- and C-termini and loop 2.

claim: The homologous partner of twin Flucs exhibits excess positive charge on loops 1 and 3.

claim: Singleton Flucs display relatively balanced charge distributions on either face.

claim: A balanced Arg+Lys distribution in loops indicates dual-topology oligomeric construction.

claim: Eukaryotic Fluc genes code for a pair of homologous Fluc sequences within a single open reading frame.

claim: Bpe with solvent-accessible lysines on loop 2 (R68K), on the C-terminus (R130K), or on both do not cross-link.

claim: Laf-TM has high selectivity for F− over Cl−.

claim: Functional Fluc channels are built with the two 4-TM subunits or domains in antiparallel transmembrane topology.
